title: Gears: Trading Speed for Strength
description: You can't get more speed and more strength for free from the same motor — but you can trade one for the other, precisely, with two meshing wheels of teeth.

content.value: A gear is just a wheel with teeth. Mesh two of them together and turning one forces the other to turn too — but not necessarily at the same speed. A small gear driving a bigger one has to spin around several times for every one turn of the bigger gear, since it has fewer teeth to hand off per rotation.

content.title: ⚙️ Resize both gears
content.hint: Make the driving gear small and the driven gear big. Then swap it — make the driving gear big instead.

content.value: Here's the part that isn't optional: a motor has a fixed amount of mechanical power to give. Gearing it down (small gear driving a big one) trades away speed for extra torque — the output turns slower, but pushes harder. Gearing it up does the opposite: faster output, weaker push. You can shape the trade, but you can never get more of both at once from the same motor.

small drives big   -->  output SLOWER, but STRONGER  (gearing down)
big drives small    -->  output FASTER, but WEAKER    (gearing up)

ARIA's wheel motors are geared down: real torque matters more
than raw speed for getting a chassis moving from a stop.

This is exactly why a bicycle has multiple gears: a low gear (small in front, big at the back wheel) trades speed for the extra push needed to climb a hill; a high gear does the reverse for flat, fast riding. Same trade-off, same physics, a completely different-looking machine.

Key takeaway: meshing gears trade rotational speed for torque, in a fixed ratio set by their tooth counts. A motor's total mechanical power doesn't change — gearing only decides how that power is split between speed and strength.

quiz.question: A small 10-tooth gear drives a large 30-tooth gear. What happens to the output speed compared to the input?
options: It's 3× slower, but with roughly 3× the torque
Speed and torque are unaffected by tooth count
quiz.explain: The small driving gear has to turn 3 times for every 1 turn of the big driven gear — that ratio trades speed for torque.

quiz.question: Why does ARIA's wheel motor use a gearbox that gears the output down (slower, stronger)?
options: It's cheaper to manufacture that way
Getting a chassis moving from a stop needs real torque more than it needs raw speed
Gearboxes always slow things down regardless of design
quiz.explain: A small hobby motor spins fast but weak on its own — gearing down trades some of that speed for the torque actually needed to move a robot.

quiz.question: Can gearing give a motor both more speed AND more torque at the same time?
options: No — gearing only redistributes the motor's fixed mechanical power between speed and torque
Only with a very expensive gearbox
quiz.explain: It's a trade, not a bonus. Whatever speed you gain, you lose in torque, and vice versa — the total power available doesn't change.
